0.title: Do Not Be Shaken
0.overview:
Second Thessalonians was written from Corinth only weeks or months after the first letter — probably in the autumn of AD 51. Paul had received further news from Thessalonica, and it was concerning. Someone — perhaps a forged letter, perhaps a claimed prophecy — had convinced some in the congregation that 'the day of the Lord has already come' (2:2). The eschatological excitement of the first letter had curdled into eschatological anxiety, and in that anxiety some had stopped working altogether, apparently reasoning that if the day was upon them, there was no point in continuing with ordinary life.

Paul writes with unusual urgency to address both the false teaching and its practical consequences. His response to the doctrinal error is one of the most detailed accounts of events preceding the Second Coming in the New Testament — the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the restrainer, the strong delusion. His response to the practical error is one of the most direct ethical instructions in all his letters: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat. The two problems are connected: a false eschatology produces disordered living; a true eschatology produces ordered, purposeful, patiently working discipleship.

Did Paul write this letter? Some scholars doubt it, because it is so like 1 Thessalonians in wording yet seems to speak differently about the end: there the day comes suddenly, here certain events must come first. But the letter was received as Paul’s from the earliest days, it closes with his own signature, This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine (3:17), and the two pictures fit together: the day will surprise the unprepared, yet God has set what must precede it. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it, within months of the first letter, to correct a misunderstanding of it.

The letter is framed by two great convictions. The first is the righteous judgment of God (chapter 1): those who afflict the Thessalonians will face divine retribution; those who are afflicted will receive relief. The God who sees the suffering of his people does not leave it unanswered. The second is the faithfulness of God (chapter 3): 'The Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one' (3:3). Between the sovereign judgment of the first chapter and the guarding faithfulness of the last runs the most extraordinary theological disclosure of the letter — the mystery of lawlessness, the restrainer, and the man of lawlessness whose coming precedes the Lord's. Paul does not explain everything; he explains enough to steady the congregation and call them back to the settled, working, praying life of those who know their God and wait for his Son.

1.title: Relief Is Coming
1.overview:
Within months of his first letter, Paul writes again. The persecution in Thessalonica has grown worse, someone is claiming (perhaps in Paul’s name) that the day of the Lord has already come, and some believers have stopped working. Chapter 1 steadies a suffering church before any correction comes.

Paul thanks God that their faith and love are growing under pressure, and says their endurance is itself evidence that God is at work. Then he answers the question suffering always raises: will wrong go unanswered? No. When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, God will give relief to the afflicted and justice against those who reject him, who will be shut out from his presence. On that day Christ will be glorified in his people. Paul prays that God will make them worthy of that calling, by his power and grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church, again describing it as living in God the Father and the Lord Jesus, and wish them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why a Second Letter So Soon

Within months the Thessalonians were being told, possibly under Paul's own name, that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2), and the idleness the first letter warned about had hardened. Paul lays the foundation first: grace and peace from God our Father — and everything hard in the letter sits inside that frame (3:16, 18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church squeezed by hostility outside and a rumour inside is first told where it is: in God our Father.

Now: A frightened congregation cannot hear correction until it has been steadied, and the steadying is doctrinal rather than emotional.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians was written a few months after the first letter, because the church faced worsening persecution, confusion about the day of the Lord, and continuing idleness among some members. Chapter 1 addresses the persecution. Paul thanks God that their faith and love are growing and boasts of their endurance (vv. 1–4). Their suffering is evidence of God’s just judgement: he will count them worthy of his kingdom, and repay their persecutors (vv. 5–6). This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, punishing those who do not know God or obey the gospel with eternal destruction away from his presence, and being glorified among his saints (vv. 7–10). So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling and fulfil their every good purpose, so that Christ’s name is glorified in them (vv. 11–12). The chapter teaches the justice of God, the certainty of judgement, and the hope of the persecuted.

Setting and background. Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth around AD 51 (Acts 18:11). Some had been unsettled by a claim, perhaps in a forged letter, that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2). Others had stopped working (3:6–12).

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. Key words. The same three as in the first letter.

To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Our Father”: the warm addition compared with 1 Thessalonians 1:1.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Grace and peace come equally from the Father and the Son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was at peace outwardly. They were persecuted. But God’s peace was theirs.

In a sentence. From Paul, Silas and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace and peace to you from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whatever pressures you face, God’s grace and peace are yours today.
verseByVerse.note: Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth, to a church still under persecution and now confused about the day of the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says thanksgiving for them is a debt he owes God, because their faith is thriving and their love for one another is growing, and he holds up their perseverance under persecution as an example to other churches. Their suffering is a sign that God judges rightly and counts them fit for his kingdom. God will repay their persecutors and give his afflicted people rest when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels in flaming fire. Those who refuse to know God or obey the gospel will suffer everlasting ruin, cut off from the Lord’s presence and glory, on the day he comes to be honoured among his people. So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of their calling and by his power bring every good intention and work of faith to completion, so that Jesus is honoured in them and they in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Justice

Recompense is grounded in God's justice, not his temper (v.6), and ekdikesis is a just penalty imposed by the one authorised to impose it — which is why Christians may never take revenge (Rom 12:19). Verse 9's ‘eternal destruction’ has been read by conditionalists as final cessation and by the historic Reformed majority as unending ruin; both readings agree that its heart is exclusion ‘from the presence of the Lord’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The promise of judgment was given to persecuted people not as a licence for revenge but as its removal: let God judge, and endure.

Now: This doctrine is written for patience, not satisfaction, by a man with unceasing anguish for those outside (Rom 9:2-3); and on that day the exhibit is the saints themselves (v.10).

verseByVerse.quote: We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.

We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right. Key words. “Ought” (opheilō, owe, are obligated). Thanksgiving is a debt owed to God.

Because your faith is growing abundantly. Key words. “Growing abundantly” (hyperauxanō, growing beyond measure). Paul had prayed for this (1 Thessalonians 3:10). God answered.

And the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Key words. Every one: no exceptions. Paul prayed for increasing love (1 Thessalonians 3:12); God answered that too.

Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God. Key words. Paul tells other churches about them.

For your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring. Key words. Steadfastness (hypomonē, endurance). Persecution had not destroyed their faith; it had strengthened it. Present tense: the afflictions were continuing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution is good. It means God uses it to grow faith.

In a sentence. We ought always to thank God for you, brothers and sisters, and rightly so, because your faith is growing more and more, and the love all of you have for one another is increasing. Therefore, among God’s churches we boast about your perseverance and faith in all the persecutions and trials you are enduring.

For worship. Thank God for believers whose faith grows under pressure. Pray for persecuted churches.

verseByVerse.quote: This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—

This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God. Key words. “Evidence” (endeigma, proof, sign). Their faithful endurance under persecution is evidence that God judges rightly: he is at work in them, preparing them, and he will vindicate them.

That you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God. Key words. “Considered worthy” (kataxioō, counted worthy). Not that suffering earns the kingdom, but that God, by grace, counts them worthy, and their endurance shows the genuineness of their faith.

For which you are also suffering. Key words. They suffer because they belong to God’s kingdom (Acts 14:22). Suffering for the kingdom is a mark of belonging to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by suffering. It is by grace. But those saved by grace endure, and their endurance is evidence.

In a sentence. All this is evidence that God’s judgement is right, and as a result you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering.

On a Tuesday. If you suffer for Christ, see it as evidence that you belong to his kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels
verseByVerse.commentary:
since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels

Since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you. Key words. God’s justice requires that persecutors be repaid. Not personal revenge (Romans 12:19), but God’s right judgement.

And to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us. Key words. “Relief” (anesis, rest, release, loosening). God will give rest to his suffering people. Paul includes himself.

When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven. Key words. “Revealed” (apokalypsis, unveiling). Now hidden from sight, Christ will be unveiled publicly at his return.

With his mighty angels. Key words. Literally, the angels of his power. They accompany him as his army (Matthew 13:41; 25:31).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should seek revenge. They leave it to God.

In a sentence. God is just: he will pay back trouble to those who trouble you and give relief to you who are troubled, and to us as well. This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels.

For worship. If you have been wronged for your faith, entrust it to God. He is just and will give you rest.

verseByVerse.quote: in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.

In flaming fire. Key words. Fire symbolises God’s holy presence and judgement (Exodus 3:2; 19:18; Isaiah 66:15; Daniel 7:9–10).

Inflicting vengeance. Key words. “Vengeance” (ekdikēsis, just punishment, justice). Not spite, but justice done. Christ himself carries it out.

On those who do not know God. Key words. Those who have refused the knowledge of God available to them (Romans 1:18–21, 28).

And on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus. Key words. The gospel is a command as well as an offer: repent and believe (Acts 17:30). Refusing it is disobedience.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God judges people for what they could not know. Everyone has rejected some light from God.

In a sentence. He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Obey the gospel today: trust and follow Christ. And pray for those who do not.

parallels.desc: the LORD will come in fire

verseByVerse.quote: They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,

They will suffer the punishment. Key words. “Punishment” (dikē, penalty, justice). What they deserve.

Of eternal destruction. Key words. “Eternal” (aiōnios, age-long, everlasting): the same word used for eternal life (Matthew 25:46). “Destruction” (olethros, ruin, loss). Not annihilation but ruin, the loss of everything good.

Away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might. Key words. “Presence” (literally face). The essence of hell: shut out from the face of God, the source of all joy, light and life (Matthew 25:41; 7:23). Separated from his favour, though not from his justice.

Where Christians differ: eternal punishment or annihilation? Some (annihilationists or conditionalists) argue that eternal destruction means the wicked cease to exist, a destruction whose results are eternal. Universalists say all will eventually be saved. Verdict: Eternal destruction is everlasting, conscious ruin: exclusion from God’s gracious presence forever. The same word “eternal” describes both the punishment of the wicked and the life of the righteous (Matthew 25:46). Scripture speaks of the smoke of their torment rising forever and ever (Revelation 14:11; 20:10), and of unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43–48). This is the historic Christian teaching (Westminster 33.2). It is terrible, and should move believers to tears and to urgent evangelism, as it moved Paul (Romans 9:2–3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in punishment (Ezekiel 33:11). It means he is just, and sin is infinitely serious.

In a sentence. They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might

For worship. Thank Christ that he bore the punishment you deserved. Pray for those still facing it.

parallels.desc: from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty

verseByVerse.quote: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.

When he comes on that day. Key words. The day of the Lord.

To be glorified in his saints. Key words. Christ’s glory will be seen in his people, as what he has made them reflects his glory. “In” his saints: they will show his glory.

And to be marveled at among all who have believed. Key words. Believers will marvel at him, overwhelmed with wonder. Echoes Psalm 89:7 and 68:35.

Because our testimony to you was believed. Key words. The Thessalonians will be among them, because they believed Paul’s gospel. A personal assurance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be glorified apart from Christ. His glory is reflected in them.

In a sentence. on the day he comes to be glorified in his holy people and to be marvelled at among all those who have believed. This includes you, because you believed our testimony to you.

For worship. One day you will marvel at Christ. Begin to marvel at him now in worship.

verseByVerse.quote: To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

To this end we always pray for you. Key words. With that day in view.

That our God may make you worthy of his calling. Key words. “Make worthy” (axioō, count worthy). God called them; may he make them live up to it (Ephesians 4:1).

And may fulfill every resolve for good. Key words. Every good desire and purpose they have, God completes (Philippians 2:13).

And every work of faith by his power. Key words. Every action springing from faith (1 Thessalonians 1:3). By his power: not theirs.

So that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him. Key words. Mutual glory: Christ glorified in them, they glorified in him. His name: his person and reputation.

According to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. All by grace. Some read it as “our God and Lord, Jesus Christ,” calling Jesus God directly; the Greek can be taken either way. Either way, grace from both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean worthiness is earned. God makes us worthy by grace.

In a sentence. With this in mind, we constantly pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling, and that by his power he may bring to fruition your every desire for goodness and your every deed prompted by faith. We pray this so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer for yourself and someone you love: that God would fulfil every good desire and work of faith by his power.

2.title: The Mystery of Lawlessness
2.overview:
Someone had told the Thessalonians, perhaps by a forged letter in Paul’s name, that the day of the Lord had already come. To a persecuted church promised relief on that day (1:7), this was devastating: either the promise had failed, or they had been passed over. Paul answers with an argument they can check: the day cannot have come, because two things must happen first, the great rebellion and the revealing of the “man of lawlessness”, who sets himself up in God’s place. Something now restrains him; when it is removed he will appear, deceive those who refused to love the truth, and be destroyed by the Lord Jesus with a breath.

Paul had taught this in person (v. 5), so he writes in shorthand, and some details (above all the restrainer) are now uncertain. The pastoral point is plain: the worst coming evil is held back now, runs on God’s timetable, and ends effortlessly at Christ’s coming. So Paul turns to thanks: God chose them, the Spirit sanctifies them, and glory awaits. Stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some had alarmed the church by claiming, perhaps in a letter falsely attributed to Paul, that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul tells them not to be shaken. That day will not come before a great rebellion and the appearance of the man of lawlessness, who will oppose God, exalt himself above every object of worship and claim to be God. Something is restraining him for now, until it is removed. Then he will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth and the splendour of his coming. His arrival will be Satan’s work, with false signs and wonders that deceive those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth, so God gives them over to the lie they preferred.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judicial Hardening

God sends the delusion of verse 11 ‘therefore’ — because they refused to love the truth (v.10). It is a judicial response to a prior refusal, and it locates the failure in the affections, not the intellect: which is also why signs and wonders prove nothing on their own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The claim that the day had already come was devastating to a persecuted church promised relief on that day (1:7); and Paul's language is allusive because he had taught them this in person (v.5).

Now: Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess — and the six verses of build-up end with the Lord undoing the lawless one with a breath (v.8). The proportions are the message.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must not be shaken by claims that the day of the Lord has already come.

Picking up the first letter. “Coming” is parousia (1 Thessalonians 4:15). “Gathered together” is episynagōgē, the scene of 1 Thessalonians 4:17: the dead raised and the living caught up to meet him. That teaching had been twisted.

Shaken and alarmed. The first verb is used of a ship torn from its moorings; the second describes ongoing agitation. Knocked off the foundations, then kept rattled: what false teaching does to a church.

Three channels. A prophecy in the meeting, a sermon or report, or a forged letter. Paul does not know which. Hence he signs this letter himself (3:17). Apostolic mail was being counterfeited within twenty years of the resurrection.

Has come. A perfect tense: already here. Not “near”, which Paul taught, but arrived and missed.

Why devastating. They were promised relief “when the Lord Jesus is revealed” (1:7). If this was the day, still hunted and still burying friends, the promise had failed or they had been passed over.

A secret rapture first? Pretribulational Christians hold the church will be removed before the day of the Lord, and the lawless one appear only afterwards. But Paul treats the coming, the gathering and the day as one event, and tells the church it will see the rebellion and the lawless one first (v. 3). The more likely reading is one public return, at which Christ gathers his people and judges the lawless one (v. 8).

On a Tuesday. When a frightening claim about the end times goes round your church or your feed, test it against what Scripture actually taught.
verseByVerse.note: Someone was claiming — perhaps even by a forged letter — that the day of the Lord had already come.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day will not come until the rebellion and the revealing of the man of lawlessness.

A checkable argument. Paul does not reason from feelings. Certain things must happen first; plainly they have not; so the day has not come. Any frightened believer could run it.

The rebellion. Hē apostasia, with the article: a specific, expected event. The word means defection; the Greek Old Testament uses it for turning from God. Most likely a great falling away within the professing church, as Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:10–12) and Paul warns (1 Timothy 4:1): the climax of a defection already at work (v. 7).

Revealed. Apokalyptetai, the word used of Christ’s appearing (1:7). A dark mirror of the real unveiling.

Lawlessness. His principle is the abolition of God’s law and any authority above himself.

Son of destruction. A Hebrew idiom: he belongs to ruin. The only other person so called is Judas (John 17:12).

Who is he? Three main answers: a Roman emperor of Paul’s day; a succession of rulers or an institution (the Reformers identified the papacy, seeing a church that put its authority in God’s place); or a single final figure. Paul describes one person, revealed and then destroyed at Christ’s coming (v. 8). The more likely reading is a final individual, the fullest form of a rebellion with many forerunners: “many antichrists have come” (1 John 2:18).

A textual note. Many manuscripts read “man of sin” (KJV). The earliest read “man of lawlessness”; the meaning is close, since “sin is lawlessness” (1 John 3:4).

A caution. Every confident identification across twenty centuries has so far been wrong. Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess.

verseByVerse.quote: who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will oppose God and exalt himself, even claiming to be God.

Against every object of worship. Not a rival religion but the abolition of religion, clearing the field so that only he is left to be worshipped.

Daniel’s pattern. “The king … shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods” (Daniel 11:36). Daniel’s first fulfilment was Antiochus Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up an altar to Zeus in the temple: “the abomination that makes desolate” (Daniel 11:31; compare Mark 13:14).

Recent memory. About ten years before, the emperor Caligula had ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple; war was narrowly avoided by his death. Everyone knew the story.

Takes his seat. He does not merely enter; he sits, as on a throne.

Which temple? Three readings: the Jerusalem temple; the church, which Paul calls God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16); or a picture of usurping God’s place. Dispensational Christians expect a rebuilt temple, but the New Testament nowhere promises one. The more likely reading is that he sets himself up in God’s place within the sphere of worship, perhaps inside the professing church.

The oldest temptation. “You will be like God” (Genesis 3:5), accepted publicly. Every self that sets itself above all authority is made of the same material.

For worship. The true God took the opposite road: he “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7).

parallels.desc: exalt himself and magnify himself above every god

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul had already taught them this.

Not new. Paul is reminding, slightly exasperated, not introducing.

Why it is allusive. He writes “the rebellion” and “what restrains” without explanation because they had heard him explain it. We hear one side of a conversation whose other half was spoken in a Macedonian house and never written down.

Honest limits. So the restrainer was obvious to them and is obscure to us. Anyone claiming certainty is claiming to have recovered that conversation.

Teaching new believers. Paul was in Thessalonica for a few weeks (Acts 17:2), working night and day (1 Thessalonians 2:9), yet he taught brand-new converts the sequence of the last things. He did not treat it as advanced material to be held back.

On a Tuesday. Teach new believers the whole story, including Christ’s return. A church taught well is hard to panic.

verseByVerse.quote: And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something is restraining the lawless one until his time, though the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.

Neuter, then masculine. In v. 6 the restrainer is “what restrains” (to katechon); in v. 7 “he who restrains” (ho katechōn). Paul moves between a force and a person.

The proposals. (1) The Roman state and the rule of law, God’s servant against anarchy (Romans 13:1–4); that would explain why Paul writes guardedly, since predicting the empire’s removal was dangerous. (2) The preaching of the gospel, or Paul’s mission. (3) God himself, or an angel such as Michael, who stands guard in Daniel 12:1. (4) The Holy Spirit through the church.

The likeliest. Paul himself died long ago and the restraint continues. The most likely answer is the restraining power of law and order that God has set over the world, held in his hand and removed at his time. The Spirit is never removed from the world.

A rapture argument? Dispensational Christians say the restrainer is the Spirit in the church, removed at the rapture. But Paul never says so, and the lawless one is destroyed at the same coming at which believers are gathered (vv. 1, 8).

Already at work. “Mystery” means hidden, not yet disclosed. What will finally appear in one figure is already operating underground.

What is certain. Evil is now held back. The world, bad as the news is, is not evil at full strength. Someone has a hand on it. And even the final rebellion is revealed “in his time”, on God’s timetable.

For worship. Thank God tonight for the evil he is restraining that you never see.
verseByVerse.note: No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; suggestions include the rule of law, the Roman empire, and the preaching of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he is revealed, the Lord Jesus will destroy him by his appearing.

No battle. After six verses of build-up, it is over in half a sentence. The Lord does not draw a sword; he exhales.

Isaiah 11:4. Of the Messiah: “he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.” Pneuma is breath, wind and spirit (compare Revelation 19:15).

By his appearing. The epiphaneia of his parousia: not by what he does on arriving, but by arriving. Darkness undone when a shutter opens.

The proportions are the message. Whatever this power is, it is not in the same category as the one who ends it.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read simply “the Lord”, others “the Lord Jesus”. Either way it is Christ.

On a Tuesday. When evil looks unstoppable, remember how this chapter ends: with one breath.

parallels.desc: with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lawless one comes with Satan’s power and false wonders, deceiving those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth.

His parousia. The royal-visit word Paul uses of Christ. The counterfeit runs down to the vocabulary.

Power, signs and wonders. The very trio used of Jesus’ ministry (Acts 2:22). Here they are false: signs pointing somewhere untrue.

Miracles prove nothing alone. Deuteronomy 13:1–3: if a prophet’s sign comes true and he says “let us go after other gods”, do not listen. Jesus: false christs will perform great signs (Matthew 24:24). The test of a message is never its power, but its truth.

Refused to love the truth. Not “failed to understand” or “were never told”. The problem is in the affections. Truth was available and they did not want it, a condition no amount of evidence cures (John 3:19).

And so be saved. Loving the truth was the road out, and it was open. They declined a rescue.

On a Tuesday. Ask God not only to make you know the truth, but to make you love it, even when it is inconvenient.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives them over to the lie they preferred, so that those who delighted in unrighteousness are condemned.

God sends it. Hard, and not to be softened.

Therefore. Everything depends on it. This follows v. 10: because they refused the truth. A judicial response, not an opening move on neutral people. No one here wanted the truth and was prevented.

The biblical pattern. Pharaoh hardened his heart, and God hardened it (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). In Romans 1 God three times “gave them up” to what they had chosen. Judgment is God ceasing to obstruct a person’s own direction of travel (compare 1 Kings 22:19–23).

Had pleasure. They did not merely disbelieve; they enjoyed the alternative. Paul traces unbelief to what people love.

What it does not mean. Not God deceiving the innocent, nor a diagnosis to pronounce on neighbours. It comforts a church wondering how so many could be taken in: God is not absent even from that.

For the anxious. If you fear this describes you, your fear is evidence against it. These people do not want the truth and are content. Wanting it is the opposite condition, and the beginning of the road out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By contrast Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians, loved by the Lord, because God chose them for salvation through the Spirit’s sanctifying work and their belief in the truth, calling them through the gospel to share Christ’s glory. So they must stand firm and hold on to the teaching they received, by word or letter. Paul prays that the Lord Jesus and God the Father, who loved them and gave them eternal comfort and good hope by grace, will encourage their hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and the Means It Arrives By

Verse 13 compresses the whole of salvation into one Trinitarian sentence — God chose, the Spirit sanctified, they believed, and glory lies ahead — and verse 14 refuses to let election float free of the means: it reached them ‘through our gospel’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After the lawless one and the delusion, what Paul asks for is undramatic: stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

Now: A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic — and what eschatology is for is steadiness in ‘every good work and word’ (v.17).

verseByVerse.quote: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God that he chose them for salvation through the Spirit’s sanctification and belief in the truth, calling them through the gospel.

But. A total reversal, point for point. They refused the truth; you believed it. They were given delusion; you were sanctified by the Spirit. They are condemned; you are bound for glory. Comfort for a frightened church.

The Trinity in one sentence. God chose, the Spirit sanctifies, and the glory is the Lord Jesus Christ’s.

A textual note. Manuscripts divide between aparchēn, “firstfruits” (early converts of the region), and ap’ archēs, “from the beginning” (chosen in eternity). The words look almost identical. The ESV prefers firstfruits; NIV and KJV prefer “from the beginning”. Either way, God’s choice came first.

What kind of election? Arminian Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul says God chose them “to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth”: faith and holiness are the means God chose to bring them to salvation, not the reason he chose them (Ephesians 1:4; 2:8).

Through our gospel. Election never floats free of the means. It reached them through three men preaching in their town (1:10).

How do I know I am chosen? Not by peering into God’s secret decree, but by what God has done: if you believe the truth and the Spirit is making you holy, you bear the marks of his choice.

Glory given. The lawless one grabs at God’s place (v. 4). These receive glory as a gift.

For worship. Before you chose him, he chose you.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they must stand firm and hold to the apostolic teaching.

After all that. The apostasy, the lawless one, the delusion, and what Paul asks is undramatic: stand, and hold.

Stand firm. A soldier holding position (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Not working out the timetable.

Traditions. Paradosis, what is handed over: the word Paul uses of the Lord’s Supper and the resurrection (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:3). Apostolic teaching in transit, not accumulated custom.

Word or letter. Paul puts his preaching and his writing on the same level: one of the earliest signs that apostolic writing carried the authority of apostolic speech.

Unwritten tradition? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches cite this verse for oral tradition carried in the church alongside Scripture. But the traditions here are the apostles’ own teaching, not later custom, and the spoken teaching was the same gospel they wrote down. We now have it only in their writings, to which Paul himself points (3:14). Scripture tests every later tradition.

The answer to the crisis. Shaken by a spirit, word or letter (v. 2)? Not a new revelation, but: go back to what you were taught.

On a Tuesday. A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic. Know your Bible.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” here means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, whether in person or in writing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May Christ and the Father, who loved us and gave eternal comfort and good hope by grace, comfort and establish them.

One action. Two subjects, the Son and the Father, with singular verbs, as in 1 Thessalonians 3:11. Jesus is named first. Not argued, simply the shape of Paul’s praying.

Past tense first. He loved us, he gave us. The request rests on what is already done.

Eternal comfort. Their comfort had been shaken; what they have been given outlasts what shakes it.

Good hope. An expectation with grounds, not wishful thinking.

Establish. To prop up what is leaning, what Timothy was sent to do (1 Thessalonians 3:2).

Work and word. After twelve verses on the man of lawlessness, the goal is not correct end-times charts but steady deeds and speech. That is what eschatology is for.

For worship. The future is not a threat to God’s people. It is held by the one who loved us.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers,<sup>2</sup>not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.<sup>3</sup>Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,<sup>4</sup>who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.<sup>5</sup>Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?<sup>6</sup>And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time.<sup>7</sup>For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.<sup>8</sup>And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.<sup>9</sup>The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders,<sup>10</sup>and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.<sup>11</sup>Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false,<sup>12</sup>in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.<sup>13</sup>But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.<sup>14</sup>To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>15</sup>So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.<sup>16</sup>Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace,<sup>17</sup>comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

3.title: The Lord Is Faithful
3.overview:
Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord will run ahead, and assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them. Then he deals firmly with a problem that has grown since his first letter: some believers, probably excited about Christ’s return, have stopped working and are living off others while meddling in everyone’s business. Paul had worked night and day to support himself as an example, and had taught them, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.”

The church must withdraw ordinary support and fellowship from such people, so that they are brought to their senses, yet treat them as brothers, not enemies. Those who have carried the load must not grow weary of doing good. The letter ends with peace, Paul’s own signature against forgery, and grace for all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to pray that the Lord’s message will spread and be honoured as it was with them, and that the missionaries will be rescued from wicked people, since not everyone has faith. But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen and protect them from the evil one. Paul is confident they are doing what he commands, and prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faithless, and Faithful

‘Not all have faith’ — ‘but the Lord is faithful’ (vv.2–3): Paul answers human faithlessness not with a better estimate of people but with a reliable Lord, who promises not exemption from trouble but to establish and guard his people through it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul wrote from Corinth, where Acts 18 records exactly the ‘wicked and evil men’ of verse 2.

Now: Confidence placed ‘in the Lord about you’ (v.4) survives disappointment, because it never rested on the people themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks for prayer that the word may spread quickly and the apostles be delivered from wicked people.

Pray for us. The apostle asks a harassed young church to pray for him, in letter after letter.

Speed ahead. Literally “run”, echoing Psalm 147:15: “his word runs swiftly”. He asks for the message to move, not for the messenger to be comfortable.

Be honoured. Received for what it is, not heard and shelved (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

As among you. Frightened, confused, troubled by idlers, and still his example of the gospel running well.

Wicked and evil men. “Perverse”: people with whom argument does not work. Paul wrote from Corinth, where Acts 18:12–17 records a united attack and a trial before Gallio.

Not all have faith. Paul does not assume all opposition is misunderstanding. Some do not believe, and that has consequences for those who do.

On a Tuesday. When you meet real hostility for your faith, do not assume you must have handled it badly. Pray for missionaries, and pray that the word runs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord is faithful and will establish and guard them from the evil one.

Faithless, faithful. “Not all have faith … but the Lord is faithful”: the same root set against itself. The answer to human unreliability is not better people but a reliable Lord (1 Corinthians 1:9; 2 Timothy 2:13).

Establish. Stērixei, to prop what is leaning: the fourth time in these letters (1 Thessalonians 3:2, 13; 2 Thessalonians 2:17), now as a promise to people shaken (2:2).

Guard. A sentry’s word.

The evil one. Or “evil”; most take it personally after chapter 2’s account of Satan’s work. The Lord’s Prayer petition (Matthew 6:13), answered as a statement.

What it does not mean. Not exemption from trouble; Paul has just said they will not be spared it. A promise to be held and guarded through it. That is the only assurance Scripture gives.

A textual note. A few manuscripts read “God is faithful”. “The Lord” is better attested.

For worship. Every promise God has made to you rests on what he is, not what you are.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident they will obey, and prays that the Lord will direct their hearts to God’s love and Christ’s steadfastness.

Confidence before correction. Hard instructions are coming, and Paul prepares the ground. Anyone who must correct someone should copy this.

In the Lord about you. Not in their track record, which had wobbled. Confidence in the Lord at work in people survives disappointment, because it never rested on them.

Direct. Kateuthynai, to clear a road: used in 1 Thessalonians 3:11 of Paul’s journey. Here the road runs through the heart.

Love of God, endurance of Christ. Both ambiguous: God’s love for us or ours for him; the endurance Christ showed or the endurance he gives. They run together. We learn to love God by being brought into his love, and endure by drawing on the one who endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2–3).

On a Tuesday. Staying power is not manufactured by resolution. When you are tired, look at Christ’s endurance and ask for a share of it.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–15 – Idleness, and How to Deal With It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul commands them, in the Lord’s name, to keep away from any believer who lives in idleness, refusing to work. The missionaries themselves set the example: they did not eat anyone’s food without paying, but worked hard night and day so as not to burden anyone, not because they had no right to support, but to give a model to copy. Their rule was that anyone unwilling to work should not eat. Some are idle busybodies; they must settle down and earn their own living. The others must not grow tired of doing good. Anyone who ignores this letter is to be noted and avoided, so that he is ashamed, yet treated as a brother to be warned, not as an enemy.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discipline That Aims at Restoration

Verses 14 and 15 must be held together: the withdrawal is real, and its aim is the offender's own recovery; and he is still to be warned as a brother. Drop the firmness and the church helps nobody; drop the warmth and discipline becomes expulsion.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul could command the idle to work only because he had worked night and day in front of them, declining support he had every right to (vv.7–9).

Now: Verse 10 is about the unwilling, not the unable, and it governs the church's own table. And verse 13 speaks to the faithful who have carried more than their share: do not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must keep away from any believer who lives in idleness, against the apostolic teaching.

Command. In the first letter Paul asked and urged (1 Thessalonians 4:1; 5:14). Now he commands, in Christ’s name. The problem has hardened.

Idleness. Ataktōs, a soldier out of rank. Members who had stopped working, almost certainly because of excitement about Christ’s return, and were relying on others.

A brother. Not outsiders or the poor, but fellow believers.

Keep away. To draw back, shorten sail. Not expulsion; v. 15 calls him still a brother. What is withdrawn is the ordinary support and easy fellowship that made the behaviour sustainable. Feeding a man who will not work pays him to stay as he is.

The tradition. As in 2:15. A way of life can contradict apostolic teaching as surely as a doctrine.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “that they received”, others “that you received”. The sense is the same.

On a Tuesday. Love sometimes means stopping help that is enabling harm. Do it kindly, and keep talking.
verseByVerse.note: The problem of idleness in the church is now worse than when Paul wrote the first letter.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles worked night and day to set an example, not because they had no right to support.

Checkable. Almost word for word 1 Thessalonians 2:9. Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), working before dawn and after dark.

Toil and labour. Kopos and mochthos: exhaustion and grind.

The right. Paul argues elsewhere that preachers should be paid: “the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14). He gave up the right here for a reason.

What it does not mean. Not that ministers should never be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18).

An example. Typos, the stamp. He deliberately worked harder than necessary to leave a shape to copy.

The only footing. When Paul tells the idle to work, everyone knows he already did it in front of them.

On a Tuesday. Before you ask others to change, ask whether your own life gives you the right to.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is unwilling to work should not eat.

Unwilling. The key word. Not those who cannot find work, cannot work, or cannot get enough. The settled refusal of someone able, here for supposedly spiritual reasons, while eating at a poor church’s expense.

What it does not mean. Not indifference to the poor. This is the man who organised a great collection for poor believers (2 Corinthians 8–9), who said “do good to everyone” (Galatians 6:10), and that neglecting your household denies the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Using this verse against the needy uses it against its author.

We kept saying it. Standing instruction from the start, not new severity.

The church’s table. Paul tells the church what to do with its own resources, not a government what to do with citizens. Refusing to subsidise a choice is not abandoning a person.

A failure of love. The idle man’s food comes from his brothers (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12). The rule defends the poor.

Work is good. Not a curse but part of being human (Genesis 2:15); Christ himself was a carpenter (Mark 6:3).

verseByVerse.quote: For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idle busybodies must work quietly and earn their own living.

A pun. Mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous: not working but “working around”, minding everyone else’s business.

Idleness is never idle. The energy is redirected into other people’s affairs. In a small church that does real damage (1 Timothy 5:13).

Command and encourage. Firm and warm at once.

Quietly. As in 1 Thessalonians 4:11. The cure for meddling is not a rule against gossip; it is a job.

Their own bread. Echoing v. 8: do what Paul did.

On a Tuesday. Retired, between jobs or underemployed? Fill your hours with useful service, or they will fill themselves with something worse.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: not busy at work (ergazomenous) but busybodies (periergazomenous).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The others must not grow weary of doing good.

The second casualty. Not the busybodies, but the faithful who have carried more than their share, watching others eat at the common table. That is wearying, and Paul names it.

Lose heart. When disorder is tolerated, the orderly wonder why they bother. That corrosion damages a church more than the idleness itself.

What Paul does not say. He does not tell them to police the others or to hold back their own good work until it is sorted. Simply: keep going, “for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

On a Tuesday. If you have been faithful for years with little to show and have started to calculate, this is a hand on your shoulder: do not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who disobey should be noted and shunned, so that they feel ashamed, yet still warned as brothers.

Take note. Name the matter openly rather than gossiping privately.

Have nothing to do with him. Withdraw ordinary fellowship and support (v. 6).

Ashamed. Not humiliated, but brought up short: seeing how his conduct looks. In a community where he truly belongs, that is a mercy, because it changes him (compare 2 Corinthians 2:6–8).

Not an enemy. Still a brother. “Warn” is noutheteō: correction aimed at change.

Both halves. Drop the firmness, and the church tolerates anything and helps no one. Drop the warmth, and discipline becomes expulsion with no road home (compare Matthew 18:15–17; Galatians 6:1).

On a Tuesday. If you must distance yourself from a believer for a time, keep praying for him and keep the door open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the Lord of peace will give them peace at all times and in every way, and be with them all. He adds a greeting in his own handwriting, the mark of every genuine letter from him, and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord of Peace, and a Signature Against Forgery

Only here does Paul write ‘the Lord of peace’, saying of Christ what a Jew would say of God; and his handwritten signature (v.17) answers the forged letter of 2:2 with a test the church can actually use.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To a year-old, harassed congregation Paul wrote of flaming fire and the son of destruction, and signed off with grace.

Now: ‘All’, twice in three verses (vv.16, 18), puts even the disciplined inside the blessing — the difference between discipline and rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the Lord of peace give them peace at all times and in every way.

The Lord of peace. Elsewhere “the God of peace” (Romans 15:33; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Only here “the Lord of peace”, meaning Jesus: another unargued place where Paul says of Christ what a Jew would say of God.

Himself. Not a technique for calming down. A gift he hands over (John 14:27).

At all times, in every way. No moment and no circumstance excluded, “however it has to come”.

Where this sits. After persecution, forgery, panic, the lawless one and church discipline. Not peace as the absence of trouble, but given in the middle of it.

All. Including the idle of v. 6 and the one marked in v. 14. The difference between discipline and rejection, in one word.

For worship. Ask the Lord of peace for his peace in the specific thing troubling you today.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul signs with his own hand, as in every letter.

The pen changes hands. Paul dictated his letters (Tertius wrote Romans, Romans 16:22) and signed them himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11).

Why it matters here. The trouble began with “a letter seeming to be from us” (2:2). So Paul gives a test they can use: genuine letters carry his hand.

Practical remedies. He answers forgery not only with argument (chapter 2) but with a procedure. Pastors with only theology and no practical help leave their people defenceless.

Every letter. Writing very early, Paul already expects his letters to circulate and to be worth counterfeiting.

Protecting Scripture. The written half of “the traditions” (2:15) had to be guarded, and this is how.

On a Tuesday. Check sources before you share a claim that seems to come from an authority.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed off in his own hand — a safeguard against forgeries such as the one hinted at in 2:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends with grace for all of them, including the idle.

All, again. The second time in three verses. Those to be withdrawn from are inside the blessing.

No hostility. Flaming fire, eternal ruin, withdrawal of fellowship: none of it was written against anyone. It was written to hold a church together and bring its wanderers back.

The frame. Grace opened the letter (1:2) and closes it. Everything between sits inside.

Who received it. A few dozen former pagans and synagogue-goers, perhaps a year old, harassed and confused, quarrelling over who should work. Paul wrote to them about the glory of the Lord Jesus, and signed off with what would get them through the week.

A textual note. Many manuscripts add “Amen”, as scribes often did.

For worship. Grace is the one provision that does not run out.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you,<sup>2</sup>and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.<sup>3</sup>But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.<sup>4</sup>And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command.<sup>5</sup>May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.<sup>6</sup>Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.<sup>7</sup>For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you,<sup>8</sup>nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you.<sup>9</sup>It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.<sup>10</sup>For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.<sup>11</sup>For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies.<sup>12</sup>Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.<sup>13</sup>As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.<sup>14</sup>If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed.<sup>15</sup>Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.<sup>16</sup>Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.<sup>17</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.<sup>18</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
